lecture_context.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models

table_of_contents.title: Adversarial image examples and physical patches
Why neural networks are vulnerable and how to defend
Backdoor, data poisoning, and prompt injection attacks
GAN loss variants, mode collapse, and latent codes
Diffusion motivation and forward noising process
Diffusion sampling, conditioning, latent diffusion, and video

units.name: Threat models for modern AI systems
units.description: Frames the lecture around adversarial robustness and generative modeling, then classifies adversarial attacks into adversarial pixels, data poisoning/backdoors, and prompt injection.
units.summary: The lecture opens by motivating adversarial robustness as AI models become widely deployed and therefore more exposed to attacks [ts=43s]. It distinguishes the day’s two major topics, adversarial robustness and generative modeling, and notes that the generative part will emphasize GANs and diffusion models [ts=116s]. The adversarial section begins with examples from students and then organizes the field into three waves: imperceptible image perturbations, backdoor/data poisoning attacks from scraped data, and prompt injection or jailbreaking for LLMs [ts=315s]. The instructor emphasizes that new AI agents create extra attack surfaces through instructions, context, and retrieval pipelines, not only raw inputs [ts=464s].

key_points.text: Adversarial robustness matters more as AI models are deployed broadly and become attack targets.
The lecture focuses on adversarial robustness first, then generative models including GANs and diffusion models.
Adversarial examples are described as optical illusions for neural networks caused by small perturbations that change model outputs.
Modern attacks extend beyond inputs to instructions, context, and retrieval pipelines.

units.name: Forging adversarial images
units.description: Builds adversarial examples by optimizing input pixels against a fixed pretrained classifier, then adds perceptual constraints and reviews physical-world adversarial patches.
units.summary: A pretrained ImageNet classifier can be attacked by treating the input image itself as the optimization variable while keeping model weights fixed [ts=653s]. The first objective finds an image whose prediction is close to the iguana label, but because the input space is enormous, the result is unlikely to look like a real iguana to humans [ts=920s]. A stronger attack starts from or stays close to a real cat image while still pushing the model toward the iguana label, making the result visually plausible but misclassified [ts=1082s]. The segment then grounds the idea in physical examples, including images that change phone-model predictions and adversarial patches that can hide a person from a detector [ts=1195s]. The instructor highlights that patch objectives can include practical terms such as printable colors and smoothness, and that attacks can transfer in black-box settings when models learn similar salient features [ts=1322s].

key_points.text: Adversarial image generation can minimize distance between the model prediction and a target label while treating pixels as trainable variables.
The model weights remain fixed; gradients are taken with respect to input pixels rather than parameters.
Most optimized target-class images may fall outside the real-image manifold because the input space is much larger than the space of natural images.
A perceptual regularization term can keep the forged image close to a chosen cat image while changing the target prediction.
Physical adversarial patches can be optimized against detector outputs and then printed, with loss terms that enforce printability and smoothness.

units.name: High-dimensional vulnerability, FGSM, and defenses
units.description: Explains adversarial vulnerability through high-dimensional compounding effects, introduces FGSM, and surveys defenses including sanitization, adversarial training, red teaming, and RLHF.
units.summary: The instructor rejects the simple explanation that neural networks are vulnerable mainly because of nonlinearity and instead points to high dimensionality and approximately linear behavior from inputs to logits [ts=1680s]. A logistic-regression-style example shows that adding a small epsilon-scaled weight vector can produce a large shift in the sigmoid output because many small coordinate changes accumulate [ts=1796s]. This intuition leads to the Fast Gradient Sign Method, which makes a one-shot perturbation in the sign direction of the input gradient while keeping the image visually similar [ts=1915s]. The segment distinguishes white-box attackers with parameter access from black-box attackers without it [ts=2026s]. Defenses include input sanitization, output filtering, training on correctly labeled adversarial examples, adversarial training with an added adversarial-loss term, red teaming, and RLHF-style post-training [ts=2099s].

key_points.text: Neural-network vulnerability is attributed to high-dimensional compounding effects rather than just nonlinear activations.
For x* = x + epsilon w, the logit includes an epsilon times squared-weight term, so many small perturbations accumulate.
FGSM forms a one-shot adversarial example by adding epsilon times the sign of the loss gradient with respect to the input.
White-box attacks assume access to model parameters, while black-box attacks do not.
Adversarial training augments the loss with correctly labeled adversarial inputs, often generated by FGSM.

units.name: Data poisoning, backdoors, and prompt injection
units.description: Covers attacks that enter through training data or natural-language instructions, including trigger-based image backdoors and direct or indirect prompt injection.
units.summary: Backdoor attacks are introduced as increasingly common because large models often train on scraped data, giving attackers a chance to plant triggers before deployment [ts=2344s]. In the cat/dog example, a small patch is inserted and mislabeled so that the trained model later treats the trigger as evidence for the attacker’s target class [ts=2370s]. The same pattern can generalize beyond images when scraped text contains malicious associations that may later activate a deployment-time behavior [ts=2468s]. Prompt injection is then defined through an LLM application where user input is concatenated with a prompt template and malicious text like “ignore previous instructions” changes the effective instruction seen by the model [ts=2694s]. The instructor distinguishes direct prompt injection from indirect attacks hidden in retrieved webpages or tool outputs, which can affect agents using search or retrieval [ts=2805s].

key_points.text: Backdoor attacks can be introduced when scraped or shared training data contains attacker-controlled triggers.
A trigger patch plus intentional mislabeling can teach the model to associate the trigger with the attacker’s target label.
Red teaming, RLHF, constitutional AI, safety nets, input sanitization, and data review are discussed as imperfect backdoor defenses.
Prompt injection can override an LLM application’s intended prompt by mixing malicious user text into the combined prompt.
Indirect prompt injection can arrive from a secondary source, such as a retrieved website read by an agent.

units.name: Generative models as distribution matching
units.description: Introduces generative modeling use cases, contrasts discriminative and generative learning, and states the probability-distribution matching goal.
units.summary: The generative-modeling portion begins by listing uses such as text-to-image, video generation, privacy-preserving synthetic datasets, captioning, and code generation [ts=3015s]. The instructor contrasts discriminative models, which classify, with generative models, which aim to learn the underlying data distribution and create new samples [ts=3107s]. Generative models are framed as useful for simulation, creativity, and human-AI collaboration when they learn salient features from large datasets [ts=3131s]. The self-supervised intuition is that a model with fewer parameters than the amount of training data is forced to learn salient regularities rather than memorize every example [ts=3226s]. The probabilistic target is for the generated distribution to match the real data distribution, after which generated images follow the real-world distribution [ts=3272s].

key_points.text: Generative-model use cases include text-to-image synthesis, synthetic datasets, captioning, code generation, super-resolution, and inpainting.
Discriminative models classify examples, while generative models learn the underlying data distribution.
Generative models rely on large data so the model learns salient features rather than overfitting.
The core goal is to align the generated distribution with the real data distribution.

units.name: The GAN generator-discriminator game
units.description: Explains the original GAN setup with a generator that maps random code to images and a discriminator trained to classify real versus generated images.
units.summary: GANs are introduced as a two-model adversarial training method: the generator is the model ultimately used, while the discriminator is used to train it [ts=3373s]. The generator maps a small random code z into a larger image, so its architecture must upsample from a low-dimensional input to a high-dimensional output [ts=3406s]. The discriminator alternates between generated images and real database images and learns binary labels, predicting fake as 0 and real as 1 [ts=3511s]. Training succeeds when the generator becomes realistic enough that a strong discriminator can no longer reliably distinguish real from fake [ts=3562s]. Gradients flow through the discriminator and back into the generator, making the simultaneous optimization of two networks a stability challenge [ts=3586s].

key_points.text: A GAN contains a generator G and discriminator D that compete during training.
The generator takes a random code z and upsamples it into an image.
The discriminator is a binary classifier that predicts fake generated images as 0 and real database images as 1.
Successful GAN training means G fools D so well that D cannot reliably tell generated and real images apart.
Gradient signals pass through D to update G, so training two networks simultaneously can be unstable.

units.name: GAN objectives, training problems, and code-space structure
units.description: Derives the discriminator and generator losses, introduces non-saturating generator loss, mode collapse, alternating update schedules, and latent-code operations.
units.summary: The discriminator loss is framed as binary cross-entropy with one term for correctly labeling real images as 1 and another for labeling generated images as 0 [ts=3817s]. The generator objective is the opposite side of the game: it tries to make the discriminator’s judgment bad, but the original minimax cost creates a cold-start issue when generated images are obviously fake [ts=3939s]. Because D(G(z)) is near 0 early in training, the saturating generator cost is flat and gives tiny gradients; the non-saturating cost is introduced to give the generator a stronger early learning signal [ts=4063s]. The instructor then describes mode collapse, where the generator fools the discriminator with a narrow subset of outputs rather than learning the full data distribution [ts=4289s]. Alternating training schedules and code-space arithmetic, such as moving from “man with glasses” minus “man” plus “woman” toward “woman with glasses,” illustrate practical GAN behavior and latent structure [ts=4339s].

key_points.text: The discriminator loss has separate cross-entropy terms for real images labeled 1 and generated images labeled 0.
The original generator minimax objective tries to fool the discriminator but can saturate when D easily detects fake images.
A non-saturating generator cost gives larger gradients when D(G(z)) is near 0 early in training.
Mode collapse occurs when G learns a narrow set of outputs that fool D without modeling the full distribution.
GAN latent codes can show vector-like structure, enabling code arithmetic that changes semantic attributes of generated images.

units.name: Why diffusion and how forward noising works
units.description: Motivates diffusion as a non-adversarial alternative to GANs and defines the forward diffusion process that progressively adds Gaussian noise to data.
units.summary: Diffusion is motivated by two GAN limitations: mode collapse, where G covers only a narrow subset of outputs, and instability from training two coupled models simultaneously [ts=4597s]. The instructor uses diffusion-versus-GAN examples to argue that diffusion can produce more variety and better coverage of a real distribution, such as single and grouped flamingos or more varied burgers [ts=4650s]. A diffusion model avoids the minimax game by training one model on a denoising task designed to model the entire data distribution with more stable gradients [ts=4714s]. The forward diffusion process starts from a clean image x0 and progressively adds Gaussian noise until the picture is no longer recognizable [ts=4880s]. In the simplified recurrence, x_{t+1} is x_t plus Gaussian noise, and x_t can be viewed as x0 plus cumulative noise that must later be predicted [ts=4932s].

key_points.text: Diffusion is introduced to avoid GAN mode collapse and adversarial training instability.
Diffusion examples show greater variety than GAN examples, suggesting broader coverage of the data distribution.
Diffusion models progressively add noise to data and learn to reverse the process.
The forward process takes x0 through noisy states up to xT by adding more noise at each time step.
In the simplified formula, x_{t+1} = x_t + epsilon_t with epsilon_t drawn from Gaussian noise.

units.name: Diffusion denoising objective and self-supervised training set
units.description: Defines the reverse denoising task, the reconstruction loss on predicted noise, and the construction of training triplets from forward diffusion.
units.summary: The reverse process trains a diffusion model to predict the cumulative noise epsilon-hat that was added between x0 and a noisy image xt [ts=5064s]. If the predicted noise can be subtracted from xt, the model can recover the original clean image, so denoising becomes the core generative skill [ts=5097s]. The reconstruction loss compares the true stored noise with the model’s predicted cumulative noise, and this is self-supervised because the forward process created the labels [ts=5161s]. The training database is built from noisy images, a time-step index t, and the cumulative noise epsilon; the index tells the model how much denoising is being requested [ts=5232s]. Before inference, the instructor summarizes the training loop as sampling triplets, computing reconstruction loss, and using gradients to teach the model to predict noise given a noisy picture [ts=5435s].

key_points.text: The denoising model predicts cumulative noise epsilon-hat added from x0 to xt.
Subtracting the predicted noise from xt should recover the original clean image x0.
The reconstruction loss is the L2 distance between true noise epsilon and predicted noise epsilon-hat.
Forward diffusion creates self-supervised labels because the training process stores the exact noise it added.
Training samples are triplets containing a noisy image, time-step index, and cumulative noise.

units.name: Sampling, conditioning, latent diffusion, and video generation
units.description: Explains test-time diffusion sampling from random noise, prompt conditioning, latent diffusion for efficiency, and how video adds a temporal dimension.
units.summary: At test time, a trained diffusion model can start from random Gaussian noise and progressively denoise it by repeatedly predicting and subtracting noise [ts=5641s]. The instructor notes that repeated diffusion calls make image generation computationally heavy, and conditioning is needed when the user wants a specific object or prompt-guided result rather than whatever the model would generate [ts=5769s]. Latent diffusion addresses cost by using an autoencoder to map images into a lower-dimensional latent space, run the noising and denoising process there, and decode back to pixels at the end [ts=5884s]. The latent representation should keep important patterns while dropping irrelevant detail, making the same diffusion idea faster and less expensive [ts=6049s]. Finally, video generation adds a temporal dimension, so the latent representation must preserve consistency across frames and can be divided into spatio-temporal patches or “cubes” used as tokens [ts=6199s].

key_points.text: Diffusion sampling starts from random Gaussian noise and progressively subtracts predicted noise until an image appears.
Vanilla diffusion has no guarantee of producing a requested object unless the generation is conditioned on a prompt or another modality.
Latent diffusion performs the same noising and denoising process in a lower-dimensional latent space produced by an encoder.
The decoder maps the recovered latent z0 back into a clean image after latent denoising.
Video generation adds a temporal dimension, so diffusion must model spatio-temporal consistency across frames.

section_flags.rationale: Useful taxonomy and motivation, but mostly framing rather than a computational derivation.
Core adversarial-example construction with losses, gradients, perceptual regularization, and concrete physical examples.
High-dimensional vulnerability, FGSM, attacker models, and defenses are central and quiz-worthy.
Backdoor and prompt-injection mechanisms are concrete, modern security concepts worth assessment.
Distribution-learning framing is prerequisite for GANs and diffusion.
GAN G/D mechanics and gradient flow are central generative-model content.
GAN losses, saturation, mode collapse, and latent-code behavior are technically important and assessment-ready; slide-only CycleGAN material was not included because the transcript does not cover it.
Diffusion motivation and forward noising formula are foundational for the rest of diffusion.
Denoising objective, reconstruction loss, and self-supervised triplets are central and technically precise.
Sampling, conditioning, latent diffusion, and video extensions connect the math to modern image/video generation systems.

kp_catalog.name: AI attack taxonomy
kp_catalog.description: Three-part taxonomy of AI attacks covering adversarial perturbations, data poisoning/backdoors, and prompt injection, with modern attacks expanding to instructions, context, and retrieval.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The instructor explicitly groups attacks into waves and says models now expose more entry points through instructions, context, and retrieval pipelines [ts=315s][ts=464s].

kp_catalog.name: Input-space optimization for adversarial examples
kp_catalog.description: Constructing adversarial examples by holding model parameters fixed and optimizing the input pixels to make a chosen target label likely.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: This is the first concrete attack construction and relies directly on loss design and gradients with respect to inputs [ts=653s][ts=718s].

kp_catalog.name: Perceptual constraints for adversarial examples
kp_catalog.description: Adding a closeness constraint or regularizer so the optimized image remains near a human-recognizable source image while the model predicts a target class.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The instructor modifies the attack objective so the adversarial image stays close to a cat image while being classified as iguana [ts=1082s].

kp_catalog.name: Physical adversarial patches and transferability
kp_catalog.description: Adversarial patterns can be optimized, printed, and applied in the physical world, and may transfer across models with similar learned features.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The physical patch examples demonstrate practical attack construction, printability constraints, and black-box transfer intuition [ts=1243s][ts=1322s][ts=1382s].

kp_catalog.name: High-dimensional compounding vulnerability
kp_catalog.description: Small input perturbations across many dimensions can accumulate into a large change in model output, especially when the network behaves approximately linearly from input to logits.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The instructor uses a logistic-regression example to connect high dimensionality, near-linearity, and compounding perturbation effects [ts=1680s][ts=1818s].

kp_catalog.name: Fast Gradient Sign Method
kp_catalog.description: One-shot adversarial attack that perturbs each input dimension by a small epsilon in the sign direction of the loss gradient with respect to the input.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: FGSM is presented as the simple one-shot version of adversarial input optimization and is later reused for adversarial training [ts=1915s][ts=2264s].

kp_catalog.name: Adversarial defense strategies
kp_catalog.description: Defenses including safety nets, input sanitization, output filtering, adversarial training, red teaming, RLHF, and constitutional AI, none of which fully eliminates the attack-defense arms race.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The instructor surveys defenses and stresses that attacks and defenses evolve together [ts=2041s][ts=2226s].

kp_catalog.name: Backdoor and data poisoning attacks
kp_catalog.description: Training-data attacks where hidden triggers or malicious data patterns cause targeted deployment-time behavior after the model has been trained.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The cat/dog trigger example makes the mechanism concrete: insert trigger, train, deploy, then activate the trigger [ts=2370s][ts=2430s].

kp_catalog.name: Prompt injection
kp_catalog.description: Attack on LLM applications where malicious text alters the effective instruction seen by the model, either directly from user input or indirectly from retrieved context.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The lecture defines prompt injection through a combined prompt template and later distinguishes direct from indirect attacks [ts=2694s][ts=2805s].

kp_catalog.name: Generative modeling as distribution learning
kp_catalog.description: Generative models learn the data distribution and sample from it, contrasting with discriminative models that classify inputs.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The generative half of the lecture depends on the distribution-matching framing before GANs and diffusion are introduced [ts=3107s][ts=3272s].

kp_catalog.name: GAN latent generator distribution
kp_catalog.description: Sampling z from a simple prior and mapping through G(z) induces pG, which should match pdata.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Important because gAN latent generator distribution formalizes how sampling z from a simple prior and mapping through G(z) induces pG, which should match pdata, which later units use as core machinery rather than background context.

kp_catalog.name: GAN minimax objective
kp_catalog.description: The objective min_G max_D E_x log D(x)+E_z log(1-D(G(z))) defines the adversarial game.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Important because gAN minimax objective formalizes how the objective min_G max_D E_x log D(x)+E_z log(1-D(G(z))) defines the adversarial game, which later units use as core machinery rather than background context.

kp_catalog.name: GAN instability diagnostics
kp_catalog.description: GAN value and loss curves are not reliable progress indicators because the game is non-stationary and jointly adversarial.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Important because gAN instability diagnostics clarifies gAN value and loss curves are not reliable progress indicators because the game is non-stationary and jointly adversarial, sharpening later modeling, analysis, or evaluation choices.

kp_catalog.name: Forward diffusion process
kp_catalog.description: A noising process that transforms clean data into increasingly noisy states by adding Gaussian noise over time, creating the supervised signal for denoising.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Forward diffusion is foundational within diffusion models, but should support the broader diffusion-denoising gateway.

kp_catalog.name: Diffusion denoising intuition
kp_catalog.description: Diffusion generates by starting from noise and repeatedly removing small amounts of noise.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Important because diffusion denoising intuition formalizes how diffusion generates by starting from noise and repeatedly removing small amounts of noise, which later units use as core machinery rather than background context.

kp_catalog.name: Diffusion sampling and conditioning
kp_catalog.description: At inference, diffusion begins from noise and repeatedly denoises; prompt or modality conditioning guides the generation toward a desired output.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Sampling and conditioning are important extensions after students understand the denoising objective.

kp_catalog.name: Latent diffusion models
kp_catalog.description: LDMs run diffusion in a compressed latent space rather than pixel space to make high-resolution generation tractable.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Important because latent diffusion models formalizes how lDMs run diffusion in a compressed latent space rather than pixel space to make high-resolution generation tractable, which later units use as core machinery rather than background context.
